stem: Two small charges exert an electrostatic force of magnitude F on one another. Both charges are doubled and their separation is doubled. What is the new force?
explanation: By Coulomb’s law, F is proportional to q₁q₂/r². The numerator increases by four and the denominator by four, giving F.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025). The teacher-provided D.2 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme were used as difficulty/style benchmarks.

stem: A neutral metal sphere gains 3.0 × 10¹² electrons from a negatively charged rod. What is the charge acquired by the sphere? (e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
sourceNote: Original item aligned to the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025). The teacher-provided D.2 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme were used as difficulty/style benchmarks.

stem: Which measured value could represent the net charge on an isolated oil drop in a Millikan-type experiment? (e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C)
explanation: Net charge occurs in integral multiples of e: −4.8 × 10⁻¹⁹ C = −3e.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025). The teacher-provided D.2 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme were used as difficulty/style benchmarks.

stem: A negatively charged rod is brought near a neutral, insulated metal sphere without touching it. The sphere is then earthed while the rod remains nearby. After the earth connection is removed, what is the net charge on the sphere?
options: Negative, because electrons enter from Earth
Zero, because there was no contact with the rod
Positive, because electrons flowed from the sphere to Earth
Negative, because protons moved into the sphere
explanation: The negative rod repels electrons from the sphere into Earth. Disconnecting Earth first traps a net positive charge on the sphere.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025). The teacher-provided D.2 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme were used as difficulty/style benchmarks.

stem: Two identical positive point charges are fixed as shown. What is the resultant electric field strength at P, the midpoint?
explanation: The electric fields at P have equal magnitudes and opposite directions; their vector sum is zero.
diagramAlt: Equal positive charges eight centimetres apart with midpoint P.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025). The teacher-provided D.2 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme were used as difficulty/style benchmarks.

stem: Two charges exert an electric force of 12 N on one another in vacuum. They are placed at the same separation in a uniform medium with permittivity four times that of vacuum. What is the new force?
explanation: Coulomb’s force is inversely proportional to the permittivity. Multiplying ε by 4 reduces F to 12/4 = 3.0 N.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025). The teacher-provided D.2 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme were used as difficulty/style benchmarks.

stem: A charge of −2.0 μC experiences a force of 0.012 N to the left in an electric field. What is the electric field at the charge?
explanation: E = F/q. Magnitude = 0.012/(2.0 × 10⁻⁶) = 6.0 × 10³ N C⁻¹. A negative charge experiences force opposite the field direction.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025). The teacher-provided D.2 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme were used as difficulty/style benchmarks.

stem: Parallel plates are at potentials +180 V and 0 V, separated by 6.0 cm as shown. What is the magnitude and direction of the uniform electric field between them?
explanation: E = ΔV/d = 180/0.060 = 3.0 × 10³ N C⁻¹. The electric field points from higher to lower potential.
diagramAlt: Two parallel plates with a potential difference of 180 V and separation 6.0 cm, showing field arrows from positive to negative.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025). The teacher-provided D.2 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme were used as difficulty/style benchmarks.

stem: In a diagram of electric field lines, the lines are more closely spaced in region X than in region Y. What can be deduced?
options: Electric potential must be zero in X
The electric field is stronger in X
Charge is moving faster in X
The electric field is uniform throughout both regions
explanation: Field-line density indicates field strength. Closely spaced lines represent a stronger electric field.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025). The teacher-provided D.2 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme were used as difficulty/style benchmarks.

section: Magnetic field of a straight wire
stem: A long straight wire carries current out of the page, as shown. What is the direction of the magnetic field at point P, to the right of the wire?
explanation: Using the right-hand grip rule, current out of the page gives anticlockwise magnetic field circles. At a point to the right, the tangent direction is upward.
diagramAlt: Straight wire shown by circle and central dot, with point P directly to the right at the same height.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025). The teacher-provided D.2 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme were used as difficulty/style benchmarks.

stem: A current-carrying air-core solenoid produces a magnetic field. Which statement is correct?
options: The magnetic field inside is approximately uniform away from its ends
Magnetic field lines terminate inside the solenoid
Its magnetic field has no direction
The magnetic field outside is stronger than inside at every position
explanation: An ideal long solenoid has an approximately uniform axial field inside; field lines form closed loops.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025). The teacher-provided D.2 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme were used as difficulty/style benchmarks.

stem: Viewed from one end, current flows anticlockwise around a circular coil. What is the direction of the magnetic field at its centre?
explanation: The right-hand grip rule gives a field out of the page for an anticlockwise current.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025). The teacher-provided D.2 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme were used as difficulty/style benchmarks.

stem: Which description correctly gives the direction of electric field lines around an isolated negative point charge?
explanation: The electric field points in the direction of the force on a positive test charge, so it points towards a negative source charge.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025). The teacher-provided D.2 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme were used as difficulty/style benchmarks.

stem: Two positive point charges +q and +4q are separated by 6.0 cm. Between the charges, at what distance from +q is the net electric field zero?
explanation: Equate fields: kq/x² = k(4q)/(6−x)², so 6−x = 2x and x = 2.0 cm.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025). The teacher-provided D.2 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme were used as difficulty/style benchmarks.

stem: At the midpoint between two equal and opposite point charges, what is the resultant electric field strength and electric potential?
options: The field is zero and the potential is nonzero
The field is nonzero and the potential is zero
explanation: The field vectors point in the same direction at the midpoint and add; the scalar potentials +kq/r and −kq/r cancel.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025). The teacher-provided D.2 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme were used as difficulty/style benchmarks.

section: Electric potential of a point charge
stem: The electric potential at a distance r from an isolated positive point charge Q is +800 V. What is the potential at distance 4r from Q?
explanation: For a point charge, V = kQ/r, so quadrupling distance reduces the potential by four.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025). The teacher-provided D.2 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme were used as difficulty/style benchmarks.

stem: A positively charged, hollow conducting sphere is in electrostatic equilibrium. At a point within its empty cavity, which pair of values is correct?
options: Electric field zero; electric potential positive and constant
Electric field zero; electric potential zero
Electric field nonzero; electric potential zero
Electric field nonzero; electric potential varies with position
explanation: With no charges in the cavity, the field is zero there. The potential is constant throughout the conductor and cavity, equal to the positive surface potential relative to infinity.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025). The teacher-provided D.2 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme were used as difficulty/style benchmarks.

stem: A charge of +3.0 nC moves from a point of potential +200 V to a point of potential −100 V. What is the change in electric potential energy?
explanation: ΔU = q(V_final−V_initial) = 3.0 × 10⁻⁹(−300) = −9.0 × 10⁻⁷ J.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025). The teacher-provided D.2 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme were used as difficulty/style benchmarks.

stem: Four equal-magnitude charges occupy the corners of a square as shown. What are the net electric field and electric potential at the centre P?
explanation: The two top positive charges produce downward field at P; the bottom negative charges also produce downward field. The scalar potentials from two +Q and two −Q cancel.
diagramAlt: A square with two positive charges at its top corners and two negative charges at the bottom corners, midpoint P.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025). The teacher-provided D.2 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme were used as difficulty/style benchmarks.

stem: A proton starts from rest and moves through a potential difference of 2.5 kV under the action of an electric field. What kinetic energy does it gain?
explanation: The energy gained by a proton through 2.5 kV is qΔV = 2500 eV = 2.5 keV.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025). The teacher-provided D.2 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme were used as difficulty/style benchmarks.

stem: The graph shows the potential due to a positive point charge outside a conducting sphere. What happens to the magnitude of the electric field as the distance from the centre increases?
options: It decreases because the magnitude of the potential gradient decreases
It is constant because potential is positive
It becomes negative because the graph slopes downwards
explanation: The field magnitude is |E| = |−dV/dr|; the curve becomes less steep with increasing distance, so E decreases.
diagramAlt: Positive electric potential decreasing with distance as V proportional to 1/r.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025). The teacher-provided D.2 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme were used as difficulty/style benchmarks.

section: Electric potential energy of two charges
stem: Two equal positive point charges +Q are separated by distance r. Their electric potential energy is U. What is their potential energy when the separation is doubled?
explanation: U = kQ²/r; doubling r halves the potential energy.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025). The teacher-provided D.2 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme were used as difficulty/style benchmarks.

stem: The electric potential at the surface of an isolated charged conducting sphere of radius R is V₀. What is the potential at a point R/2 from its centre?
explanation: In electrostatic equilibrium the conductor is an equipotential; its potential is constant everywhere inside, equal to its surface potential V₀.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025). The teacher-provided D.2 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme were used as difficulty/style benchmarks.

stem: An electron is moved along an equipotential surface in a static electric field. What is the work done by the electric field?
options: Positive, because the electron is negative
explanation: The potential difference is zero along an equipotential, so work by the electric field W_field = −qΔV = 0.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025). The teacher-provided D.2 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme were used as difficulty/style benchmarks.

stem: Three identical positive point charges +Q are placed at the vertices of an equilateral triangle of side a. What is the total electric potential energy of this system, taking zero at infinite separation?
explanation: There are three distinct charge pairs, each of potential energy kQ²/a. Total energy is 3kQ²/a.
sourceNote: Original item aligned to the IB Physics guide (first assessment 2025). The teacher-provided D.2 Paper 1A questions and mark scheme were used as difficulty/style benchmarks.
